topics.title: Systems with 2 variables word problem help
topics.text:
Question: Bobo the clown always likes to wear one white sock and one black sock. If he changes his socks every day, and at the end of several days finds that he has used exactly $\frac15$ of his white socks and $\frac58$ of his black socks, what fraction of all of his socks has he used?

Solution:

The number of white socks he has used must be equal to the number of black socks he has used. Thus, if $w$ is the number of total white socks and $b$ is the number of total black socks, $\frac15w=\frac58b$, so $8w=25b$. Therefore, Bobo has $25k$ white socks and $8k$ black socks for some positive integer $k$, and $5k$ white socks and $5k$ black socks have been used. So Bobo has used $\frac{5k+5k}{25k+8k}=\boxed{\frac{10}{33}}$ of his socks.



Can someone help explain how we ended up with $5k$ white socks and $5k$ black socks? hence $5k +5k$

topics.title: k New lower bound on the value of .999...
topics.text:
Hey, everyone,

After years of deadlock in the MSM concerning this issue, I may have found valuable insight that will help us lock down the value of $.\overline{9}$ once and for all.



First of all, consider the series $1-1+1-1+...$, where the +'s and -'s alternate. As discussed at length in this forum, this sum is equal to $\frac{1}{2}$.



Now, consider the quantity $x=.9999999...$, the value which we seek to find.

Notice that $\frac{x}{11}=.090909...$, since $10\cdot .090909...+.090909...=.99999...$

Then we also clearly have that $\frac{10x}{11}=.909090...$.

Consider $\frac{9x}{11}=\frac{10x}{11}-\frac{x}{11}=\frac{9}{10}-\frac{9}{100}+\frac{9}{1000}-...$



Using Cauchy-Schwarz on $1-1+1-1+...=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{9x}{11}$, we obtain that

\[ \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{9x}{11}\ge \left(\sqrt{\frac{9}{10}}+\sqrt{\frac{9}{100}}+\sqrt{\frac{9}{1000}}+...\right)^2 \]Or

\[ \frac{9x}{22}\ge 9\left(\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}}\right)^2 \]Which simplifies to

\[ \boxed{x\ge 4.705...} \](approximately)



So we have proved that $.\overline{9}\ge 4.705...$, an astounding leap from the previous estimate of $1$.



I will continue to investigate the value of $.\overline{9}$, including by attempting to upper bound it, and will keep you posted on any results I find.

topics.title: Tough Problem from 2010 MC States
topics.text:
Source: 2010 Mathcounts State Sprint #30 ProblemPoint D lies on side AC of equilateral triangle ABC such that $m \angle DBC = 45^\circ$. What is the ratio of the area of triangle ADB to the area of triangle CDB? Express your answer as a common fraction in simplest radical form.




SolutionLet's say that $AC$ is the base. We drop a perpendicular from $B$ to point $E$ (Note that we are creating 30 60 90 triangles, so we let the height be $\sqrt{3}$, and the base be $2$). Now, we draw $BD$.  We notice that $BD$ is an angle bisector, so we may apply the angle bisector theorem: $AB/EB = AD/DE$. By 30-60-90 triangles, we have $AB/EB = AD/DE = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$. Now we calculate the ratio: We have that our total area is $\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot \sqrt{3} = \sqrt{3}$. So, the area of $BDE$ is $\sqrt{3} - \frac{2}{2 + \sqrt{3}}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)
 = 3 - \sqrt{3}$. Thus, the ratio is $\frac{3 - \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3} - (3 - \sqrt{3})} = \frac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{2}$

topics.title: Help?????
topics.text:
I don't get the following problems from the MathCounts handbook. If someone could help that would be great!



Click to reveal hidden text1) The 1990 and 2018 calendars are identical in the number of days in each month and the day of the week on which each day of each month occurs. In fact, the calendar repeats in these ways every 28 years until the year 2100. How many days are there in the 28 years preceding 2018?



2) A cubic yard of topsoil is to be spread evenly in the garden at Prove It! Math Academy. The garden measures 10 feet by 8 feet. How many inches deep will the topsoil be? Express your answer as a mixed number.



3) The square shown is divided into five cells. How many paths can be drawn that start at any cell, move only to adjacent cells and visit each of the five cells exactly once? (Diagram is first attachment.)



4) In the hardware store, Matt goes to the fastener aisle, which has wood screws, sheet metal screws, hex bolts, carriage bolts and lag bolts. How many ways can he choose 10 fasteners if he needs at least one of each kind?



5) A family farm is equally divided among three heirs: Jim, Jan and John. John’s share of the farm is then equally divided among his three heirs: Peter, Paul and Patricia. Paul decides to sell his share of the farm, and then later the family decides to sell the remainder of the farm all at once. What portion of the proceeds from the most recent sale should Jim receive? Express your answer as a common fraction.



6) In 2016 the Flying Turtles finished their baseball season with a record of 95 wins and 67 losses. The Dolphins finished the season with 84 wins and 78 losses. The Flying Turtles and Dolphins played each other 19 times during the season. If the Flying Turtles had F wins against teams other than the Dolphins, and the Dolphins had D wins against teams other than the Flying Turtles, what is the value of F + D?



7) Six semicircles, each of radius r, are constructed inside a regular hexagon of side length s, one on each side, so that each semicircle is tangent to two others. What is the ratio of r to s? Express your answer in simplest radical form. (Diagram is second attachment.)



8) Gaylon starts writing down dates from January 1, 2018 onward as follows: 01012018, 01022018, 01032018, etc. What is the 2018th digit Gaylon writes down?



9) Zeus threw, on average, 12 lightning bolts per day in the month of March. During the first week in April, he averaged 15 lightning bolts per day. How many lightning bolts does Zeus need to throw per day on average for the rest of April to maintain a 12-bolt-per-day average over March and April? Express your answer to the nearest integer.



10) The owners of two food carts calculate their weekly profits for three weeks. The medians and the highest weekly profit values are the same for the two carts. The mean weekly profit of Cart A is $27 more than that of Cart B. What is the absolute difference between the lowest weekly profit values of Cart A and Cart B?




Please send in solutions. Thanks a lot!!

topics.title: MathCounts "Probability Stretch" Problem
topics.text:
I was confused about the following problem from the MathCounts handbook because my method turned out to be wrong and I don't quite get why...



Click to reveal hidden textWhen the circuit containing blinking lights A and B is turned on, lights A and B blink

together. Then A blinks once every 5 seconds and B blinks once every 11 seconds.

Lindsey looks at the two lights just in time to see A blink alone. What is the percent

probability that the next light to blink will be A blinking alone?




My method was:

Click to reveal hidden textSince the next light to blink could be $A$ blinking, $B$ blinking, or both $A$ and $B$ blinking together, there are $3$ possibilities for what light would blink next. $A$ blinking is one of these possibilities so as a fraction, the probability of $A$ blinking is $\dfrac{1}{3}$. This approximates to 33% which was my answer...However, the correct answer is 50%  :wacko:




What is wrong with my method and what's the correct way to solve it? Thanks in advance!!   :-D

topics.title: k Does .9 repeating equal 1?
topics.text:
Many people believe that .999...=1, even the AoPS book Competition Math for Middle School says it's true. I wrote this essay about it and I wanted to have a debate. Does anyone want to debate, its fun! I take the agree side.



One very common proof uses 9th grade Algebra to prove this. They assume x is .999… and after using elementary operation they get that x also equals one therefore showing that .9… equals 1.



x=.999…

10x=9.999…

10x-x=9x

Also, 9.999…-.999=9

So, 9x=9

X=1





Another elementary proof involves fraction and decimal conversions. If you grab a calculator and type in 1 ÷ 9 you will quickly realize that you will see .1… and they go on for ever. Then if you plug in 2 ÷ 9 you will get .2.. And so on. If we continue this pattern we will see 9 ÷ 9 equals .9…

Also showing that 1 equals .9 repeating.



1/9= .111111111…

2/9= .22222222…

3/9=⅓= .33333333…

4/9= .44444444…

5/9= .55555555…

6/9=2/3=.66666666...

7/9= .77777777…

8/9= .88888888…

Then 9/9=.99999999…, So 1=.99999999…





Wolfram Alpha



One of the trusted computational knowledge engine also shows that .9… =1





















This is also an very easy proof and will work with any odd denometaried fraction. (Even denominator fractions will result in 1=1). You have to make sure that the two numerators when added together equal the denominator. So when you add the fractions they will equal one. Then you take decimal version of the fraction, a repeating decimal, and added it to the decimal version of the second fraction, another repeating decimal, and you will see that you will get .99… for every number even weird numbers like 7 and 13.



1/7=   .142857142857….

+

6/7=   .857142857142...

=      =

7/7=    .999999999999…



Also,



1/11=   .090909090909090909090909090…..



10/11= .909090909090909090909090909…..

=

11/11=  .99999999999999999999999999…..





Some people say,



.11…+.99…=1



So therefore .9… cannot be equal to be one. This is not true.





.1+.9=1

.11+.99=1.1

.111+.999=1.11

.1111+.9999=1.111

.11111+.99999=1.1111



As you can see as the number of 1’s and 9’s increase the sum gets further and further away from 1 so therefore it cannot equal 1. So what does it equal?



Well, if we kept going 1’s would be added to the ends of the sum. So therefore, .1.. +.9...=1.11…

Also, if we subtract .1… from both sides we get .9… equals 1.



.9… = 9/10+9/100+9/1000…



As you can see this is a geometric series with first term (a) of 9/10, and common ratio (r) of 1/10. Using the formula for the sum of an geometric series (which is not debatable but a formula like A=BH) which is a/1-r. If you plug in the numbers you can see that y get (9/10)/(9/10) which is equal to one. Showing you again that .9… equals 1.

Many people say that 1-.9…=0.0...1?

Well that is like saying we have infinite, never ending, supply of food and we are going to get some more food after we are done eating an infinite amount? Surely, that makes no sense.





If you do not believe that .9…=1 you believe that they are different numbers. Then you should be able to find their average or the number in between. (.9…+1)/2=? Well if you say it is.9...5 that’s wrong since, that number does not exist as proved before. Well some people say it’s one, and that helps me prove my point. If (.9…+1)/2=1, then .9…+1 =2 subtracting 1 from both sides you get .9…=1.
